documents.abstract: LLM-graded pass rates are increasingly used as outcomes when evaluating AI feedback, yet they may measure conformity to a grading specification rather than student correctness. We audited one such system, in which GPT-4o graded Python function-interface designs and, in one of two practice modes, also gave detailed advice (43 novices, AB/BA crossover, 899 submissions; two independent human coders). The grader was not invariant to construct-preserving lexical change: replacing one reference name with a human-acceptable synonym failed 47 of 100 otherwise unchanged passing variants, against 7% for unchanged copies, and in two problems the grader rejected the wording of the problem statement itself. Its errors were systematic rather than random: false passes concentrated on answers whose only defect was a type the grading prompt had been told to accept (24–39% vs 6–8% for substantive defects). Measured by the system’s own pass rate, detailed feedback outperformed pass/fail feedback (OR 4.6); measured by a uniform re-grader or by human judgement, it did not (OR 1.5 and 1.4). Which arm the system mis-measured depended on whether the human standard adopted the grader’s type rule. Effects measured by an LLM grader are properties of the specifications — problem statement, reference answer, grading prompt and human standard — as much as of the instruction. We provide an audit checklist and release the procedure, coding manual and scripts.

Human-machine systems rarely operate at a fixed level of AI autonomy. As operators and AI systems collaborate over time, control must shift: the AI can take on more responsibility when collaboration is stable, maintain its current role when evidence is ambiguous, or return control to the human when conditions deteriorate. Existing work on adaptive automation, supervisory control, trust in automation, and deskilling explains parts of this problem, but provides no auditable, multi-signal criterion for governing when autonomy should change across multi-cycle workflows. We formalise this challenge as the Handover Problem: deciding, at each operational cycle, whether to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy while keeping the process reversible, recoverable, and auditable. We introduce the Handover Readiness Score (HRS), a transparent composite measure that integrates four signal dimensions: operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, and operational performance. It is combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy that requires sustained positive evidence before increasing autonomy but reverts promptly when conditions worsen. Across software engineering and manufacturing domains, the HRS and hard safety guards address complementary failure regimes: guards enforce immediate corrective action when a single indicator breaches a critical threshold, while the HRS detects the slow, multi-signal erosion of operator readiness that no individual guard can observe. The framework establishes autonomy handover as a governance problem requiring explicit, composite, and auditable criteria. This provides a conceptual and formal foundation that adaptive automation research has not previously provided.

LLMs are evolving rapidly, with newer models offering stronger capabilities. This suggests that in LLM-based relevance judging, more capable models will achieve higher agreement with human judgements under the same prompt. We challenge this understanding by investigating the behavior of LLM-based relevance judges under backbone evolution. Keeping the prompts fixed, we evaluate a representative single-prompt (UMBRELA) and a rubric-based prompt (EXAM) across sequential model versions of commercial (Gemini, GPT) and open-weight (Qwen, Llama) models. Overall, we find no consistent evidence that newer versions lead to better relevance judges. Crucially, similar or improved aggregate performance does not imply judgment stability: correct judgements made by an earlier version of an LLM backbone are not necessarily preserved by later versions. We investigate the potential drivers of these regressions. Our findings caution against the assumption that judging prompts designed and validated for one backbone version will perform equivalently or better when the model is updated, even within the same family.

BACKGROUND: Ergonomics is fundamental to improving safety and efficiency in offices. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to assess the effect of a health education intervention on office workers' knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) regarding ergonomics and to determine their predictors. METHODS: For this intervention study, 230 office workers were split into two equal groups. A validated KAP office ergonomics questionnaire and a health education intervention were given to the intervention group, while the control group only received the questionnaire. Three months later, both groups received a post-test questionnaire. RESULTS: The post-test KAP scores of the intervention group were significantly higher than those of the control group (37.2 versus 30.9, 23.4 versus 28.3, and 17.0 versus 10.3, respectively, P < 0.05). Workers' office ergonomics knowledge, attitude, and practice scores significantly improved following the health education intervention (P < 0.05). Adequate knowledge and a positive attitude were significantly predicted by being younger (adjusted OR: 7.8 and 10.7), having a high level of education (adjusted OR: 8.9 and 2.5), using a computer (adjusted OR: 7.0 and 5.0), working long hours on a computer (adjusted OR: 3.1 and 3.0), and having a short job duration (adjusted OR: 5.2 and 12.3) within the intervention group. There was a significant positive correlation between the knowledge and practice scores (r = 0.469, P < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The outcomes of the study demonstrated that office workers who received health education had significantly enhanced their KAP after a three-month follow-up. This highlights the importance of office workers' ergonomics education to ensure workplace safety and improve their well-being and productivity. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered at the Pan African Clinical Trial Registry (PACTR) (ID: PACTR202604893125732) on 29 April 2026.

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of “telling Chinese stories well in English,” a core value orientation of college English education in the new era, college oral English teaching undertakes the dual mission of fostering language proficiency and shaping cultural confidence. This study takes the flipped classroom model as the implementation carrier, constructs a national cultural framework with three dimensions of cultural cognition, cultural expression and cultural identity, and adopts a non-equivalent control group pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design to explore its effects and mechanisms on college students’ oral English willingness to communicate (WTC). Participants include 86 non-English major freshmen from a local comprehensive university in East China, divided into an experimental group ( n = 43) receiving flipped classroom instruction integrated with the national cultural framework, and a control group ( n = 43) receiving conventional themed flipped classroom teaching. The full intervention cycle lasts 16 weeks. Data are collected through oral English proficiency tests, L2 WTC scales, national culture framework scales, structured classroom observations and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data are statistically analyzed with SPSS 26.0, and qualitative data are summarized via thematic coding. Results show that the experimental group achieves significantly higher post-test WTC scores with a large effect size. Cultural expression and cultural identity exert significant positive predictive effects on WTC, while the direct predictive effect of cultural cognition is not significant. Interview themes suggest reduced oral anxiety, enhanced self-efficacy and greater intrinsic motivation as possible explanations for these associations; mediation pathways were not statistically tested. This study verifies the facilitative effect of local cultural content on L2 WTC, providing replicable practical paradigms and empirical evidence for the ideological and political construction of college English courses and oral English teaching reform.

Introduction This study examines the influence of transformational leadership (TRL) on job satisfaction (JS) and employee performance (EP) in public sector organizations in Sierra Leone, with a focus on the mediating and moderating roles of intrinsic motivation (IM) and perceived calling, respectively. The current study contributes theoretically by integrating motivational and leadership theories in public administration contexts. Practically, this research offers actionable insights for public sector leaders and HR practitioners, advocating leadership development programs promoting TRL behaviors and strategies to align employees’ personal values with organizational missions. Methods The current research draws on self-determination theory and the concept of calling to develop and test a moderated mediation model using survey data collected from 984 employees across six public institutions. Structural equation modeling was utilized to analyze the relationships among the variables. Results Results confirm that TRL positively influences JS and EP, with IM serving as a significant mediator in both relationships. In addition, findings reveal that the indirect effects of TRL on JS and EP via IM are stronger when employees report higher levels of calling, indicating a moderated mediation effect. These findings suggest that TRL fosters IM and also creates a supportive work environment that enhances satisfaction and performance, particularly among employees who perceive their work as a calling. Conclusion By focusing on intrinsic drivers, public organizations can enhance employee outcomes without relying solely on extrinsic incentives, thereby offering a sustainable path to performance improvement in resource-constrained settings.

OBJECTIVE: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development includes 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet their integration into Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) remains underexplored. This study aims to systematically evaluate how SDG-related topics are addressed in OHS literature. STUDY DESIGN: Umbrella review. METHODS: The review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for systematic reviews and meta-analyses on SDGs and OHS. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2 and INSA tools. RESULTS: Thirteen studies were included. SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) were the most frequently addressed, followed by SDG 5 (Gender Equality). Key themes included Industry 5.0, climate change impacts on workers, informal employment, and corporate sustainability strategies. However, the evidence base is fragmented and lacks interdisciplinary integration. CONCLUSIONS: OHS is a key but under-integrated component of the SDGs framework. A coordinated interdisciplinary approach is required to align occupational health, economic policy, and environmental sustainability.

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Despite heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and talent, an estimated 70–85% of digital transformation projects fail, partly because human-focused leadership models are lacking.OBJECTIVES: This study develops and illustrates the CODE Framework, an integrative leadership model combining change management, behavioural economics, human-centred design and ethical governance.METHODS: A qualitative theoretical synthesis was combined with a comparative case study of two organisations, JPMorgan Chase and Lenovo.RESULTS: The four pillars (Clarity of Vision, Organisational Alignment, Design for Humans and Ethical Governance) proved mutually reinforcing, with measurable outcomes evident in both organisations.CONCLUSION: The framework offers leaders an integrated roadmap for artificial intelligence-driven transformation, and the case evidence is preliminary and exploratory rather than a validation.

Reasoning models allocate extra computation at inference time and present their answers as the product of deliberate thought. If this deliberation works the way dual-process accounts of human cognition suggest, longer thinking should weaken the classic decision biases that fast, intuitive judgment produces. Using 30 vignettes covering six biases (anchoring, framing, loss aversion, escalation of commitment, availability, confirmation) from an established benchmark, we run a dose-response study across four model families, pairing each reasoning model with a matched non-reasoning sibling and requesting thinking ceilings of 0, 1,024, 4,096, and 8,192 tokens, for 12,350 API calls. Because a requested ceiling is not the same as realized deliberation, we use the reasoning tokens each call consumed as the dose. First, reasoning models are not less biased than their siblings; the point estimate leans the other way in every family, but the item-level pooled contrast is not reliable (Delta = +0.031, t(29) = 1.45, p = .157). Second, bias magnitude does not reliably fall as realized deliberation grows: no slope is significantly negative, and where anything moves it is the signed score drifting further from the human direction. Third, anchoring is the only bias in the human direction (d = 1.89). Four of the other five lean the opposite way in all seven models; with five items per bias, that reversal is reliable for framing and directional for escalation of commitment, confirmation, and loss aversion, while availability is absent. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor before answering lowered anchoring on all five anchoring items, which no amount of additional thinking did, although the effect does not reach significance (p = .057). The results argue against treating test-time reasoning as a rationality guarantee and for auditing deployed models bias by bias.

Conversational Natural Language Understanding (NLU) has passed through five distinguishable technological eras: rule-based symbolic parsing, statistical and probabilistic modelling, neural sequence learning, Transformer-based pretraining, and the current large language model regime. Existing accounts of this history tend to foreground modelling advances and treat infrastructure as a supporting detail. This article argues instead that the two tracks are causally entangled: each scientific advance in conversational NLU became production-viable only once a matching infrastructure capability, spanning hardware, data pipelines, training paradigms, and serving architecture, made it deployable at scale, and each infrastructure capability in turn exposed the next scientific bottleneck. The analysis traces a specific bottleneck sequence, from combinatorial rule brittleness through representational discreteness, vanishing gradients, and sequential processing limits, to labelled-data scarcity, showing how each resolution reshaped the engineering problems that remained. A closing synthesis argues that large language models have not simplified conversational architecture; they have relocated its complexity from authoring rules and training classifiers toward orchestration, retrieval grounding, and failure isolation across distributed inference systems. The account draws on systems-architecture reasoning applied to the published research and technical-report record, rather than on a new empirical benchmark.
